senses.gloss: Sad and discouraged.
examples: She looked *downcast* when the letter finally came.
A *downcast* group of fans filed out of the stadium.
He seemed more *downcast* than angry.

senses.gloss: Looking down at the ground.
examples: She answered with *downcast* eyes.
He stood in the doorway, his face *downcast*.

contrast: Also an adverb: *We walked downhill for an hour.* And in *It's all downhill from here* it can mean either easier or worse, so the rest of the sentence has to tell you which.

senses.gloss: Going or sloping down.
examples: The last mile of the race is *downhill*.
She took the *downhill* trail back to the car.
*Downhill* skiing is the only sport he follows.

contrast: American. *Upscale* is far more common than *downscale*.

senses.gloss: Meant for people with less money; plain and cheap.
examples: They moved to a more *downscale* part of town.
The chain opened a *downscale* version of its steakhouses.
The hotel felt *downscale* next to the one on the river.

contrast: Usually an adverb (*She went downstairs*). As an adjective it only goes before a noun — never *the bathroom is downstairs* with this meaning.

senses.gloss: On a lower floor of a building.
examples: The *downstairs* bathroom is being painted.
Our *downstairs* neighbors complained about the noise.
He keeps his tools in the *downstairs* closet.

senses.gloss: Farther along a river, in the direction the water flows.
examples: The *downstream* towns were warned about flooding.
Our camp was *downstream* from the falls.

senses.gloss: Coming later in a process or a chain of business.
examples: *Downstream* costs were higher than anyone expected.
Refining is the *downstream* end of the oil business.

contrast: Also an adverb and a noun: *We drove downtown.* American — the British say *city centre*.

senses.gloss: In or belonging to the business center of a city.
examples: She works at a *downtown* law firm.
The *downtown* stores all close at six.
*Downtown* traffic is terrible on Fridays.

senses.gloss: Treated badly for a long time by people with power, and worn down by it.
examples: The novel is about the *downtrodden* mill workers of the 1930s.
She felt *downtrodden* after ten years in that job.
*Downtrodden* tenants finally took the landlord to court.

contrast: The adverb is *downward* or *downwards*: *Prices moved downward.* The adjective has no *-s* and goes before the noun.

senses.gloss: Moving or pointing toward a lower level.
examples: Sales have been on a *downward* trend all year.
He made a small *downward* motion with his hand.
The *downward* pressure on wages continued into the spring.

position: both — often after a verb: *We were downwind of the fire*

senses.gloss: In the direction the wind is blowing; on the side the wind carries smells and smoke toward.
examples: We stayed *downwind* of the deer so they wouldn't smell us.
Farms *downwind* of the plant reported the smell for years.
The *downwind* side of the island gets far less rain.

contrast: Doubles the *b* in comparison: *drabber*, not *draber*.

senses.gloss: Dull in color and not pleasant to look at.
examples: The office walls were a *drab* olive green.
Her winter coat was even *drabber* than mine.

senses.gloss: Boring and cheerless.
examples: He was tired of his *drab* little town.
The report makes life on the base sound *drab*.

form: from *Draco*, an Athenian lawgiver famous for harsh punishments

senses.gloss: Extremely harsh and severe, especially about rules or punishment.
examples: The new phone rules struck many parents as *draconian*.
Critics called the budget cuts *draconian*.
The school took *draconian* measures against cheating.

contrast: Also a noun — a person (*an Estonian*) or the language (*She speaks Estonian*).

senses.gloss: From Estonia, or belonging to its people and language.
examples: We stayed with an *Estonian* family in Tallinn.
The menu gave an *Estonian* name for every dish.
*Estonian* winters are long and dark.

senses.gloss: Cut or marked into a hard surface.
examples: The front door had an *etched* glass panel.
Their initials were *etched* on the trophy.

senses.gloss: Fixed so clearly that it cannot be forgotten or hidden.
examples: That night is *etched* in my memory.
Worry was *etched* into his face.

contrast: Also a noun: *two Ethiopians*.

senses.gloss: From Ethiopia, or belonging to its people and culture.
examples: We had dinner at an *Ethiopian* restaurant downtown.
*Ethiopian* coffee is famous all over the world.
Both of her parents are *Ethiopian*.

senses.gloss: Judging other peoples by the standards of your own, as if yours were the normal ones.
senses.ru: этноцентричный, мерящий всех по своей культуре
examples: The old textbook takes an *ethnocentric* view of history.
His remarks about the food were plainly *ethnocentric*.
The course asks students to notice their own *ethnocentric* assumptions.

senses.gloss: Having to do with where words come from and how they changed.
examples: The dictionary gives an *etymological* note for each entry.
There is no *etymological* link between the two words.
He made an *etymological* argument for the older spelling.

senses.gloss: Of Europe and Asia taken together.
examples: The *Eurasian* land mass runs from Portugal to Japan.
*Eurasian* trade routes crossed these mountains.

senses.gloss: Of mixed European and Asian descent.
examples: Her mother is *Eurasian*.
The port city had a large *Eurasian* community.

senses.gloss: Treating Europe and its culture as the center of everything.
examples: Students complained that the reading list was *Eurocentric*.
He offers a less *Eurocentric* account of the war.
The museum is rewriting its *Eurocentric* labels.

contrast: Also written *even-handed*.

senses.gloss: Treating both sides fairly and equally.
examples: The judge was *evenhanded* with both attorneys.
We need a more *evenhanded* review of the complaints.
Her coverage of the campaign was *evenhanded*.

ru: по должности, в силу занимаемой должности
position: both — before a noun, or right after it: *a member ex officio*
contrast: Also an adverb: *She serves ex officio.* Written as two words, no hyphen.

senses.gloss: Holding a position automatically because of another job you hold.
examples: The mayor is an *ex officio* member of the board.
*Ex officio* members may speak but not vote.
As treasurer, she has an *ex officio* seat on every committee.

contrast: Legal English, almost always about evidence.

senses.gloss: Showing that someone is not guilty.
examples: The defense found *exculpatory* evidence buried in the files.
Prosecutors must hand over any *exculpatory* material.
Nothing in the emails was *exculpatory*.

form: -ed — how the person feels; *exhilarating* is what causes it
contrast: The person is *exhilarated*; the thing is *exhilarating*: an *exhilarating* ride leaves you *exhilarated*.

senses.gloss: Excited and full of happy energy.
examples: We came off the roller coaster *exhilarated*.
She felt *exhilarated* by the crowd's reaction.
The runners looked tired but *exhilarated*.

senses.gloss: Made larger or wider than before.
examples: The paper ran an *expanded* version of the story.
The *expanded* stadium seats sixty thousand.
She took on an *expanded* role after the merger.

senses.gloss: Able to be understood or accounted for.
examples: Most of the difference is *explainable* by the weather.
The noise turned out to be easily *explainable*.
Researchers want *explainable* software, not a black box.

senses.gloss: Explaining facts or ideas rather than telling a story or arguing.
examples: The class teaches *expository* writing.
He cut the long *expository* passages from the script.
The first chapter is purely *expository*.

contrast: Formal. Everyday English says *off the cuff*.

senses.gloss: Spoken or done without preparation, made up as you go.
examples: She gave an *extemporaneous* speech at the reception.
His remarks were entirely *extemporaneous*.
The debate tournament has an *extemporaneous* round.

senses.gloss: Done outside the courts and without their authority.
examples: The report documents *extrajudicial* killings.
The families reached an *extrajudicial* settlement.
*Extrajudicial* detention is banned under the treaty.

contrast: Very often in the fixed phrase *not for the faint-hearted* = not for people who scare easily.

senses.gloss: Easily frightened and lacking the nerve to act.
examples: The hike along the ridge is not for the *faint-hearted*.
He was too *faint-hearted* to ask for a raise.
*Faint-hearted* investors sold everything that week.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun: *a far-left group*
contrast: Hyphenated before a noun (*a far-left candidate*), two words after a verb (*Her views are far left*). *The far left* is a noun — the people themselves.

senses.gloss: Holding political views at the extreme left end of the scale.
examples: The party expelled its *far-left* wing.
Her economics professor is *far left*.
*Far-left* and far-right groups both showed up that day.

contrast: More often a noun (*She is a freshman*). As an adjective it stands only before a noun: *freshman year*, never *the year is freshman*.

senses.gloss: Of the first year of high school or college.
examples: *Freshman* year was the hardest of the four.
He teaches a *freshman* composition class.

senses.gloss: Serving a first term in office.
examples: The bill was written by a *freshman* senator.
*Freshman* lawmakers get the worst offices in the building.

senses.gloss: Not weakened or diluted; at its full power.
examples: Take one *full-strength* tablet with food.
*Full-strength* coffee keeps me up all night.
The cleaner is too harsh if you use it *full-strength*.

senses.gloss: Born or carried for the whole normal length of a pregnancy.
examples: The baby was *full-term* and weighed eight pounds.
A *full-term* pregnancy lasts about forty weeks.
*Full-term* babies usually go home within a day.

contrast: Traditionally an insult: *fulsome praise* is so thick that it sounds fake. Many Americans now use it simply to mean *full* or *thorough*, and careful readers still object.

senses.gloss: So excessive that it sounds insincere.
examples: He thanked the host in *fulsome* terms.
The review's *fulsome* praise made me suspicious.

senses.gloss: Full and generous — a newer use, common in the press.
examples: The senator promised a *fulsome* response to the questions.
Reporters asked for a more *fulsome* account of the meeting.

senses.gloss: Able to read a little, but not well enough to handle everyday forms, signs and instructions.
examples: About a tenth of the adults tested were *functionally illiterate*.
He hid for years that he was *functionally illiterate*.
The program helps *functionally illiterate* adults fill out job forms.

contrast: *funeral* is the noun and the word you use before a noun (*a funeral home*); *funereal* means gloomy, like a funeral.

senses.gloss: Slow, dark and gloomy, the way a funeral is.
examples: The party had a strangely *funereal* mood.
He gave the news in a *funereal* tone.
The music was slow and *funereal*.

senses.gloss: Marked with deep lines or wrinkles.
examples: His *furrowed* brow told me the news was bad.
Her face was *furrowed* from years in the sun.

senses.gloss: Cut into long grooves, as a plowed field is.
examples: We walked across the *furrowed* field.
The *furrowed* ground was ready for seed.

contrast: Also a common noun (*the future*). As an adjective it goes only before a noun: *future plans*, never *the plans are future*.

senses.gloss: Happening or existing at a later time.
examples: We are setting money aside for *future* expenses.
*Future* students will use the new library.
He introduced her as his *future* wife.

contrast: Informal and slightly critical.

senses.gloss: Talking a lot, especially about nothing important.
examples: Our *gabby* neighbor kept us on the porch for an hour.
He gets *gabbier* after a beer or two.
The show has a *gabby* host who never lets a guest finish.

contrast: Also the name of the language: *She studies Gaelic.*

senses.gloss: Of the Celtic people and languages of Ireland and Scotland.
examples: *Gaelic* football is played all over Ireland.
The choir sang a *Gaelic* hymn.
He gave his daughter a *Gaelic* name.

ru: без ума (от кого-л.); выживший из ума
contrast: Informal, and only after a verb — *go gaga*, *be gaga over someone*. Never before a noun.

senses.gloss: Wildly excited about someone or something.
examples: Everyone at work went *gaga* over the new baby.
Fans are still *gaga* about the band's first album.

senses.gloss: Confused or senile — informal, and rude about an older person.
examples: He jokes that he is going *gaga* in his old age.
Grandpa isn't *gaga* — he just can't hear you.

senses.gloss: Of a galaxy or the space between stars.
examples: The telescope maps *galactic* dust.
*Galactic* distances are measured in light-years.

senses.gloss: Enormous — informal, usually about a mistake or a scale.
examples: The project failed on a *galactic* scale.
Sending that email was a *galactic* blunder.

contrast: Used about French style or character, often half-joking. *Garlic* is the vegetable — a different word.

senses.gloss: French, especially in style or character.
examples: He answered with a *Gallic* shrug.
The film has a certain *Gallic* charm.
*Gallic* cooking is the heart of the menu.

senses.gloss: Annoying and humiliating at the same time.
examples: It was *galling* to watch him take the credit.
The most *galling* part was the apology that never came.
She found his patient tone *galling*.

senses.gloss: Shocking people into action all at once.
examples: The speech had a *galvanizing* effect on the crowd.
Her arrest was a *galvanizing* moment for the movement.
The coach's few words were *galvanizing*.

senses.gloss: Having a space between the front teeth.
senses.ru: щербатый, с промежутком между передними зубами
examples: He gave us a *gap-toothed* grin.
The *gap-toothed* kid in the photo is my father.
She was *gap-toothed* until she got braces.

senses.gloss: Tasting or smelling strongly of garlic.
examples: The sauce was rich and *garlicky*.
I could eat their *garlicky* roasted potatoes all night.
His hands smelled *garlicky* for a whole day.

form: from *gastronomy* — the art of good eating

senses.gloss: Having to do with good food and cooking.
examples: The trip was a *gastronomic* tour of the coast.
The old restaurant is a *gastronomic* landmark.
*Gastronomic* magazines rated it the best in the state.

senses.gloss: Awkward and socially clumsy, especially in a way that embarrasses people.
examples: It would be *gauche* to ask what the ring cost.
He felt *gauche* among all those polished people.
Her question about the divorce was *gauche*.

senses.gloss: Designed or organized for a particular group or purpose.
examples: The class is *geared* toward beginners.
Their whole menu is *geared* to families with small kids.

senses.gloss: Ready and prepared for something, usually *geared up*.
examples: The team is *geared* up for a long season.
Stores are already *geared* up for the holidays.

senses.gloss: Made to do many ordinary jobs rather than one special one.
examples: A *general-purpose* cleaner works on most surfaces.
It's a *general-purpose* tool, not a specialist's one.
The lab bought two *general-purpose* computers.

contrast: The plural noun *genitals* names the body parts; the adjective stands before a noun: *the genital area*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the sex organs.
examples: The doctor asked about *genital* pain.
The virus can cause *genital* warts.
The chapter covers *genital* development before birth.

contrast: Also a noun: *a Gentile* = a person who is not Jewish. Usually capitalized, and not related to *gentle*.

senses.gloss: Not Jewish.
examples: He married into a *Gentile* family.
The rule applied to *Gentile* converts as well.
Most of her neighbors were *Gentile*.

ru: грузинский; из штата Джорджия; георгианский (об архитектуре)
contrast: Three different meanings share one word — the country, the American state, and the British style of the 1700s.

senses.gloss: From the country Georgia, or of its people and language.
examples: We ordered *Georgian* wine and fresh bread.
Her grandmother still cooks *Georgian* food.

senses.gloss: From the American state of Georgia.
examples: *Georgian* peaches show up in the stores in June.
He never lost his soft *Georgian* accent.

senses.gloss: Of the British style of building and furniture of the 1700s and early 1800s.
examples: They restored a *Georgian* town house.
The square is lined with *Georgian* brick fronts.

form: compound — two origins joined with a hyphen
contrast: Also a noun: *German-Americans settled this county.*

senses.gloss: Of Americans with German roots, or of the ties between the two countries.
examples: The town holds a *German-American* festival every fall.
She writes about *German-American* families in Ohio.
His grandparents were *German-American*.

contrast: *German* means from Germany; *Germanic* means from the wider language family or from an old northern culture.

senses.gloss: Of the language family that includes English, German, Dutch and Swedish.
examples: English is a *Germanic* language.
The word has a *Germanic* root, not a Latin one.

senses.gloss: Typical of Germany or of German people.
examples: The building has a heavy *Germanic* look.
Their schedule was *Germanic* in its precision.

contrast: Also a noun: *two Ghanaians*.

senses.gloss: From Ghana, or belonging to its people and culture.
examples: The place serves *Ghanaian* stews and rice.
A *Ghanaian* doctor gave the keynote talk.
Both of her parents are *Ghanaian*.

contrast: Not the verb: *She is giving a speech* is the present continuous. The adjective means generous: *a giving person*.

senses.gloss: Generous with time, help and attention.
examples: She is the most *giving* person I know.
He comes from a warm, *giving* family.
Teaching well takes a *giving* nature.

senses.gloss: Of the medieval European style of building with pointed arches and tall windows.
examples: They toured a *Gothic* cathedral in Cologne.
*Gothic* windows let in tall shafts of light.

senses.gloss: Of a dark, frightening kind of story or mood.
examples: She writes Southern *Gothic* novels.
The movie has a *Gothic* feel from the first scene.

contrast: Many deaf people prefer *deaf* or *hard of hearing* to this term.

senses.gloss: Unable to hear well.
examples: The theater has headsets for *hearing-impaired* guests.
Her younger son is *hearing-impaired*.
*Hearing-impaired* students sit near the front.

contrast: Mostly a noun — the language *Hebrew*. As an adjective it goes before a noun: *Hebrew letters*.

senses.gloss: Of the Hebrew language or of the ancient Jewish people.
senses.ru: относящийся к ивриту или к древним евреям
examples: The book has *Hebrew* letters on the cover.
He teaches a *Hebrew* class on Sunday mornings.
*Hebrew* school met twice a week.

contrast: Informal, and always after a verb: *He is hell-bent on winning.* Never before a noun.

senses.gloss: Determined to do something whatever it costs.
examples: She is *hell-bent* on finishing the degree this year.
They seem *hell-bent* on ruining the place.
He was *hell-bent* on revenge.

contrast: Also a noun: *a heuristic* = a rough rule that usually works.

senses.gloss: Working by trial, guessing and rules of thumb rather than by a proven method.
senses.ru: эвристический, основанный на пробах и правилах
examples: The program uses a *heuristic* method to narrow the search.
Teachers like the *heuristic* value of the exercise.
*Heuristic* scanning catches viruses no one has named yet.

senses.gloss: Happening or found far above sea level.
examples: The team trains at a *high-altitude* camp in Colorado.
*High-altitude* baking needs more liquid and less sugar.
He flew *high-altitude* reconnaissance planes.

contrast: Informal and disapproving, often in *get high-and-mighty with someone*.

senses.gloss: Acting as if you were better than everyone else.
examples: Don't get *high-and-mighty* with me.
He has a *high-and-mighty* way of correcting people.
She sounded *high-and-mighty* about her new title.

senses.gloss: Charging or paying a high rate of interest.
examples: He paid off the *high-interest* credit cards first.
It's a *high-interest* loan with a short term.
*High-interest* debt grows faster than people expect.

contrast: American business English; *big-ticket* is the more common form.

senses.gloss: Costing a lot of money.
examples: Stores discount *high-ticket* items after the holidays.
A new roof is a *high-ticket* repair.
*High-ticket* customers get their own salesperson.

contrast: Also a noun in the plural: *He wears high-tops.*

senses.gloss: Cut high enough to cover the ankle, of a shoe.
examples: He laced up his *high-top* sneakers.
*High-top* basketball shoes support the ankle.
She bought a pair of black *high-top* canvas shoes.

senses.gloss: Moving, or made to move, at very high speed.
examples: The wound came from a *high-velocity* round.
*High-velocity* winds tore the roof off the barn.
They tested a *high-velocity* rifle at the range.

senses.gloss: Carrying a strong electric current.
examples: Stay away from the *high-voltage* lines.
The fence warns of *high-voltage* equipment.

senses.gloss: Full of energy and excitement.
examples: She gave a *high-voltage* performance.
It was a *high-voltage* campaign from the first week.

senses.gloss: Paying a lot of interest or profit.
examples: He moved the money into a *high-yield* savings account.
*High-yield* bonds pay more because they carry more risk.

senses.gloss: Producing a large crop.
examples: The farm planted a *high-yield* variety of corn.
*High-yield* seed changed farming across the region.

senses.gloss: Of the Himalaya mountains in southern Asia.
examples: They signed up for a *Himalayan* trek.
*Himalayan* salt is pink from the minerals in it.
The book describes life in a *Himalayan* village.

contrast: Mostly a noun — the language *Hindi*. *Hindu* is the religion; the two words are often mixed up.

senses.gloss: In or of Hindi, a main language of northern India.
examples: We watched a *Hindi* movie with subtitles.
The store sells *Hindi* newspapers.
He signed up for a *Hindi* class at night.

contrast: Almost always in *the Hippocratic oath*.

senses.gloss: Of Hippocrates and the ethical promises doctors make.
examples: New doctors take the *Hippocratic* oath.
He cited his *Hippocratic* duty to the patient.
The *Hippocratic* tradition goes back to ancient Greece.

contrast: Also a noun: *Hispanics make up a third of the county.* Many people prefer *Latino* or *Latina*.

senses.gloss: Of Spanish-speaking countries, or of Americans whose families came from them.
examples: The district has a large *Hispanic* population.
She is the first *Hispanic* judge on that court.
Both of his parents are *Hispanic*.

form: compound — a whole phrase used as one adjective
contrast: Also written *hit-and-miss*.

senses.gloss: Sometimes good and sometimes bad, with no care taken to make it consistent.
examples: Service at that restaurant is *hit-or-miss*.
He takes a *hit-or-miss* approach to studying.
The results this season have been *hit-or-miss*.

contrast: Informal. Also an interjection that shows boredom: *Ho-hum, another meeting.*

senses.gloss: Dull and ordinary; nothing to get excited about.
examples: The sequel got *ho-hum* reviews.
Sales for the quarter were *ho-hum*.
It was a *ho-hum* season for a team that expected to win.

contrast: Informal and mocking — you would not use it in a formal report.

senses.gloss: Acting grand and superior.
examples: They eat at some *hoity-toity* place downtown.
Don't get *hoity-toity* about a used car.
She has a *hoity-toity* accent she picked up at school.

contrast: Also a place in Los Angeles. As an adjective it means "of the movie business", often with a hint of fake glamour: *That ending was so Hollywood.*

senses.gloss: Of the American movie industry.
examples: The novel was turned into a *Hollywood* film.
He works as a *Hollywood* agent.

senses.gloss: Flashy and artificial, the way movies are.
examples: The wedding was a little too *Hollywood* for my taste.
They gave the story a *Hollywood* ending.

senses.gloss: Made with a hologram, so the image looks three-dimensional.
examples: The card has a *holographic* sticker on the back.
A *holographic* image floated above the table.

senses.gloss: Written out by hand by the person who signed it, of a will.
examples: The state accepts a *holographic* will with no witnesses.
The court had to read his *holographic* note twice.

contrast: Also a noun and an adverb: *go home*, *stay home*. The adjective only stands before a noun: *home cooking*, *the home team*.

senses.gloss: Connected with your house or family.
examples: Nothing beats *home* cooking.
Give the nurse your *home* address.

senses.gloss: Played on your own field, or belonging to the local team.
examples: The *home* team won by three runs.
We have six *home* games left this year.

contrast: American, and almost always about food or restaurants.

senses.gloss: Cooked plainly and generously, the way food is made at home.
examples: The diner serves *home-style* cooking.
We both ordered the *home-style* meatloaf.
It's a *home-style* restaurant with enormous portions.

contrast: Also a common noun (*a good imitation*). As an adjective it stands only before a noun: *imitation leather*, never *the leather is imitation*.

senses.gloss: Made to look like something better or more expensive, and not the real thing.
examples: The bag is *imitation* leather.
They sell *imitation* crab meat by the pound.
The ring has an *imitation* diamond in it.

position: predicative only — usually *it is inadvisable to*

senses.gloss: Not a wise thing to do.
examples: It is *inadvisable* to drive in fog like this.
Changing the plan now would be *inadvisable*.
The doctor said surgery was *inadvisable* at his age.

senses.gloss: Not relevant to a particular case or group.
examples: The rule is *inapplicable* to part-time staff.
Those figures are *inapplicable* here.
The court found the old statute *inapplicable*.

senses.gloss: Not genuine, or not true to what it claims to be.
examples: The apology felt *inauthentic*.
Critics called the restaurant's tacos *inauthentic*.
He hated the *inauthentic* cheer of the ads.

contrast: Often written *Inca* instead: *Inca ruins*, *Incan ruins* — both are used.

senses.gloss: Of the Inca people who ruled the Andes before the Spanish came.
examples: They hiked four days to the *Incan* ruins.
The museum has a room of *Incan* gold.
*Incan* roads crossed the whole empire.

contrast: The noun *incense* — scented smoke — is stressed on the first syllable and is a different word.

senses.gloss: Extremely angry.
examples: Parents were *incensed* by the decision.
She was *incensed* that nobody had called her.
He grew more *incensed* with every excuse.

contrast: Formal. Everyday English says *early* or *just starting*.

senses.gloss: Just beginning, and not yet easy to see.
examples: Doctors caught the *incipient* infection early.
There were signs of an *incipient* revolt in the ranks.
She felt the *incipient* panic rising in her chest.

contrast: Also an adverb: *held incommunicado*. Never before a noun.

senses.gloss: Cut off from talking to anyone outside, by choice or by force.
examples: The prisoner was held *incommunicado* for three weeks.
He goes *incommunicado* whenever he is finishing a book.
The crew stayed *incommunicado* until the mission ended.

contrast: Nearly always in *indentured servant* or *indentured labor*, and nearly always about history.

senses.gloss: Bound by a contract to work for someone for a fixed number of years.
examples: Many colonists arrived as *indentured* servants.
The plantation ran on *indentured* labor.
She wrote a book about *indentured* workers in the Caribbean.

contrast: Also a noun — a person, or the language.

senses.gloss: From Indonesia, or belonging to its people and language.
examples: We ate at an *Indonesian* place near the market.
*Indonesian* coffee is grown mostly on Sumatra.
Her husband is *Indonesian*.

contrast: *instructional* = made for teaching (*an instructional video*); *instructive* = teaching you something useful (*an instructive mistake*).

senses.gloss: Made for teaching or used in teaching.
examples: He watched an *instructional* video on tiling a floor.
The school bought new *instructional* materials.
*Instructional* time was cut by an hour a week.

contrast: Not the same as *instructional*, which means made for teaching. A failure can be *instructive* without being *instructional*.

senses.gloss: Teaching you something useful.
examples: The comparison between the two cities is *instructive*.
It was an *instructive* failure.
Her questions were more *instructive* than the whole lecture.

senses.gloss: Important in making something happen.
examples: She was *instrumental* in getting the bill passed.
His early research was *instrumental* to the discovery.

senses.gloss: Played by instruments, with no singing.
examples: The album ends with two *instrumental* tracks.
They played an *instrumental* version of the song.

contrast: Formal, and mostly about soldiers and employees refusing orders.

senses.gloss: Refusing to obey someone who has authority over you.
examples: He was fired for being *insubordinate*.
The sergeant called the remark *insubordinate*.
*Insubordinate* behavior goes straight into your file.

senses.gloss: So annoying or unpleasant that you cannot stand it.
examples: He becomes *insufferable* when his team wins.
The heat that August was *insufferable*.
She has an *insufferable* habit of finishing your sentences.

senses.gloss: Not enough for what is needed.
examples: There was *insufficient* evidence to charge him.
The check bounced for *insufficient* funds.
One nurse was *insufficient* for a ward that size.

senses.gloss: Interested only in your own small circle and suspicious of outsiders.
examples: The town is friendly but deeply *insular*.
He grew up in an *insular* community that distrusted strangers.
The department has become more *insular* since the layoffs.

senses.gloss: Of an island.
examples: The report covers the *insular* areas of the Pacific.
*Insular* climates are milder than inland ones.
